title: How Long Does a Cut Onion Last in the Fridge?

seo.title: How Long Does a Cut Onion Last in the Fridge?
seo.meta_description: Chopped or sliced onion can be refrigerated in a sealed container for about 7–10 days at 40°F or below. Discard sooner if moldy, slimy, watery, or foul-smelling.
seo.search_intent: Know how long cut onion keeps refrigerated and which spoilage signs matter.

excerpt: A cut onion can generally be kept about 7–10 days in the refrigerator when stored at 40°F (4°C) or below in a sealed container. That range is a storage guideline, not a guarantee: mold, slime, watery breakdown, or a clearly abnormal odor are reasons to discard it sooner.
content_html:
A whole dry onion can last for weeks in a cool, ventilated place. Once cut, the situation changes: the protective skin is gone, moisture is released, and the tissue is more exposed to contamination and deterioration.

The 7–10 day estimate assumes that the onion was cut cleanly and kept properly refrigerated. It is not a guarantee that every leftover piece is fine until day ten. If the onion sat out for a long time, was handled with dirty utensils, or was mixed with other foods, its useful window may be shorter. Treat the range as a storage guideline, not a promise that overrides the actual history of the food.

The practical range: 7–10 days

The National Onion Association, citing USDA guidance, says chopped or sliced onions can be refrigerated in a sealed container for 7 to 10 days at 40°F (4°C) or below.

You do not need to aim for day 10 every time. Flavor and aroma change too, so earlier use usually gives better quality.

A clean airtight container or well-sealed bag is usually the best setup. It slows moisture loss, keeps onion odor from spreading through the refrigerator, and limits contact with other foods and surfaces. You do not need layers of wrapping. If a lot of condensation builds up inside the container, dry it and use the onion sooner because excess moisture can contribute to soft, deteriorating tissue.

How to store cut onion

  1. Use a clean airtight container.
  2. Refrigerate promptly after cutting.
  3. Do not leave it sitting at room temperature for hours.
  4. Keep it away from raw meat or seafood juices.

A sealed container also prevents the onion odor from spreading throughout the refrigerator.

A cut onion can lose some crispness or pungency without being spoiled. More concerning signs are visible mold, water-soaked or slimy areas, sunken tissue, and a clearly unpleasant odor. Trimming a dry edge can be reasonable when the rest is firm, but widespread wet deterioration is not something to rescue piece by piece. Judge the whole stored portion rather than one small dry surface.

Discard signs

Visible mold, slime, cloudy liquid, very soft watery areas, or clearly rotten odors are reasons to throw it away. Cut onion naturally smells more intense than a whole onion, so distinguish normal sulfur aroma from sour or decomposed odors.

Cutting ruptures cells and releases sulfur compounds, so the smell of stored onion can change over time. The exposed surface also loses water and may dry around the edges. Those quality changes are not identical to microbial spoilage. Separating the two helps prevent throwing out an onion just because it smells strongly like onion, while also preventing odor from becoming the only test of safety.

Cutting changes an onion even while it remains usable

A whole onion is protected by dry outer layers and a relatively closed surface. Cutting increases contact with air, moisture, hands and utensils, which is why refrigeration and a clean container matter. Even within the 7–10 day window, pieces can lose firmness, dry at the edges or transfer odor to other foods.

Those quality changes are different from mold, sliminess or a clearly abnormal smell. The date is a guide; the condition of the food can tell you to discard it sooner.

For freezing, chop or slice the onion in the form you will use later and divide it into small portions. Freezing damages cells, so thawed onion loses its raw crunch and works better in soups, sauces, casseroles, and sautés than in salads. In many cooked dishes it can go straight from the freezer to the pan. Freezing early preserves quality better than waiting until the refrigerated onion is already at the edge.

Can cut onion be frozen?

Yes. Chopped onion can be frozen for cooked dishes. It loses crispness, so it works better in soups, sauces, and sautés than in fresh salad.

Properly sealed and cold, roughly a week is reasonable; if the texture or appearance is wrong, do not let the calendar talk you into using it.

A simple routine removes much of the guesswork: date the container, keep it in a cold part of the refrigerator, and plan to use it in the next few meals. If you already know you will not use it during the week, freeze it on day one. Then the decision does not depend on remembering when you cut the onion or trying to interpret a smell many days later.

faq.question: How long does half an onion last in the refrigerator?
faq.answer: About 7–10 days is a common guideline when it is sealed and held at 40°F (4°C) or below.

faq.question: Should a cut onion be wrapped?
faq.answer: Yes. Use an airtight container or a tight food-safe wrap.

faq.question: What if the cut surface is just a little dry?
faq.answer: Minor drying can be trimmed, but mold, slime, watery decay, or a rotten odor are reasons to discard the onion.
